hints: Start by comparing the outer layers. Plant walls use a plant polysaccharide, so think what different polymer bacteria use for strength.
For viruses, forget walls. Think what the repeating coat around viral nucleic acid is built from.
For ribosomes, remember plant cells have two sizes because of organelles, while prokaryotes are simpler. What is the only size found free in prokaryotic cytoplasm?
For nucleic acids, plant and prokaryotic cells both need DNA for genes and RNA for protein synthesis. Think whether a single virus particle carries both types or just one type.
walkthrough:
External structures are made of different polymers**
Plant cell walls get strength from cellulose microfibrils. Bacterial prokaryotic walls get strength from a different cross-linked polymer called peptidoglycan, also called murein. A virus has no cell wall at all. Its outer coat is a capsid built from many protein subunits called capsomeres, so it is made of protein / polypeptides.

Ribosome size tells you cell type**
The S value is a Svedberg sedimentation unit, a measure of size and density. Eukaryotic cytoplasmic ribosomes are larger at 80S, while chloroplasts and mitochondria retain smaller 70S ribosomes from their prokaryotic origin. That is why a plant cell has both 80S and 70S. A prokaryotic cell has only the smaller 70S ribosomes. A virus has no ribosomes because it uses the host cell to make proteins.

Cells need both nucleic acids, viruses need only one**
Both plant and prokaryotic cells store genetic information as DNA and use RNA in transcription and translation, so they contain DNA and RNA. A virus particle packages only its genome for delivery, which is either DNA or RNA, not both together in the same virus.
Final answer: prokaryotic cell wall composed of peptidoglycan / murein; virus capsid composed of protein / polypeptides; prokaryotic ribosomes 70S; virus contains DNA or RNA (only one type).

hints: Think about how Vibrio cholerae leaves one person and enters another. What faecal-contaminated vehicle links sewage to the mouth?
walkthrough:
Link cholera to faecal-oral spread**
Cholera bacteria live in the intestine and are shed in faeces. An outbreak starts when faeces containing Vibrio cholerae reach other people. The classic route is untreated or raw sewage contaminating drinking water, or food / crops / seafood contaminated by that sewage.
Final answer: contaminated drinking water / untreated raw sewage / contaminated food or seafood contaminated by raw sewage.

hints: Look closely at the choleragen drawing in Fig. 6.1. Count the separate rounded subunits joined together and recall what level of structure that represents.
walkthrough:
Count chains to spot quaternary structure**
Primary structure is one amino acid sequence, secondary is folding of that chain, tertiary is the 3D shape of one chain. Quaternary means two or more separate polypeptide chains assembled together. In Fig. 6.1 choleragen is drawn as about six rounded subunits joined as one complex, so it must contain multiple polypeptides.
Final answer: choleragen is composed of more than one polypeptide chain / multiple polypeptides.

hints: Look at the receptor in the membrane in Fig. 6.1. It has a membrane part plus branching hexagon chains on the outside. What do we call membrane lipids or proteins with carbohydrate attached?
walkthrough:
Recognise the carbohydrate tag**
In Fig. 6.1 the receptor spans the membrane but has short branching chains of hexagons sticking into the lumen. Those hexagons represent sugars. A lipid with attached carbohydrate is a glycolipid and a protein with attached carbohydrate is a glycoprotein. Either type can act as a cell surface receptor for the toxin.

hints: Chloride ions are moved out against their gradient, so energy is needed. Think what phosphorylated nucleotide cells hydrolyse to release energy for all active transport.
walkthrough:
Name the direct energy donor**
Moving $Cl^-$ out of the epithelial cell through a membrane protein requires energy because it is active transport. Cells supply that energy by hydrolysing ATP to ADP and phosphate. ATP is the phosphorylated nucleotide used.

hints: First think about solutes. When many $Cl^-$ accumulate in the intestinal lumen, what happens to the water potential outside the cells compared with inside?
Now link that gradient to water movement. Through which passive process and in which direction does water follow the solute?
walkthrough:
Chloride lowers water potential outside**
Water potential is lowered by dissolved solutes. When choleragen stimulates massive exit of $Cl^-$ into the lumen, the lumen fluid becomes more concentrated, so its water potential becomes more negative / lower than the cytoplasm. In effect the cytoplasm now has the higher water potential.

Water follows by osmosis**
Water moves across the partially permeable cell membrane by osmosis from higher water potential inside the cell to lower water potential in the lumen. That is why $H_2O$ is shown leaving through a channel alongside $Cl^-$ in Fig. 6.1, causing watery diarrhoea.

Final answer: chloride ions decrease / lower the water potential of the intestinal lumen / fluid outside cells; water moves out of cells into lumen by osmosis down the water potential gradient from high to low water potential.
